highlights: On 6 September, about 12 tons of emergency medical supplies were dispatched through the International Red Cross to relieve victims in Hiroshima.
A SCAP directive of 12 October prohibited cultivation of narcotic plants, banned narcotics export, and froze all existing stocks of opium, cocaine, heroin and marijuana.
SCAP ordered the Japanese government to inventory all military medical and dental stockpiles and transfer them to the Home Ministry for distribution to civilians.
By 31 October, about 150,000 of an estimated 2,000,000 Koreans in Japan had been repatriated through Fusan, using returning Japanese shipping.
Allied air raids destroyed or damaged 1,083 civilian hospitals with 53,007 beds in 46 prefectures, about 25 percent of Japan's civilian hospitals.
Communicable disease reports through 13 October recorded 57,729 dysentery, 50,877 diphtheria, 28,787 typhoid and 1,900 typhus cases, with epidemic typhus noted among Korean laborers.
A standard prefectural Venereal Disease Control Ordinance was mandated, instituting compulsory weekly examinations and introducing penicillin therapy for high-risk groups.
Public welfare administration was disorganized: 83,502 persons received relief, and the Japanese Red Cross was to be demilitarized.

sections.summary: Notes wartime neglect of health and welfare, return of military medical stockpiles to civilian use, narcotics control, and new directives for disease reporting and hospital bed tracking.
sections.title: General

sections.summary: Describes disorganized welfare administration, 83,502 persons on relief, five social insurance programs, demilitarization of the Japanese Red Cross, and repatriation of about 150,000 Koreans.
sections.title: Public Welfare

sections.summary: Air raids damaged 1,083 civilian hospitals; 78,000 veterans were treated in military facilities. Japan has 3,335 hospitals with 356,143 beds, operating at two-thirds capacity with sufficient personnel.
sections.title: Administration of Hospitals

sections.summary: Veterinary services have collapsed. The report gives 1944 livestock census figures and 1945 animal disease outbreaks; commercial slaughter runs at 10 percent of normal and dairy sanitation is substandard.
sections.title: Veterinary Affairs

sections.summary: War devastated dental practice and equipment manufacture: 75 percent of pre-adolescent children have severe dental problems, and air raids displaced 7,000 of Japan's 23,000 dentists.
sections.title: Dental Affairs

sections.summary: Nursing education and midwife licensing are substandard; 34,000 nurses were absorbed into wartime military service, and women have no representation in nursing associations or licensing boards.
sections.title: Nursing Affairs

sections.summary: Medical supply manufacturing is paralyzed. About 12 tons of emergency supplies went to Hiroshima, military medical stockpiles moved to civilian channels, and a 12 October directive froze and controlled narcotics.
sections.title: Medical Supply

sections.summary: Reviews public health laws; a standard prefectural venereal disease ordinance brings compulsory weekly examinations and penicillin therapy. Civil service reform to elevate technical specialists over administrators is under study.
sections.title: Legal

sections.summary: Reports over 50,000 cases each of diphtheria and dysentery, epidemic typhus among Korean laborers, inadequate water chlorination, port quarantine protocols, and a nutritional target of 1,800 calories per day.
sections.title: Preventive Medicine

summary: This initial monthly summation covers non-military activities in public health and welfare across Japan during September and October 1945, representing the earliest comprehensive SCAP assessment of Japan's domestic medical and social conditions following surrender. The report documents the acute deterioration caused by wartime neglect and air raids, including damage to over 1,000 civilian hospitals, paralyzed medical manufacturing, substandard nursing and dental training, and the disruption of municipal sanitation and water treatment. Occupation authorities moved quickly to establish administrative control by issuing directives for communicable disease reporting, narcotics prohibition, weekly hospital bed censuses, and the demilitarization of the Japanese Red Cross. Key public health concerns included widespread outbreaks of diphtheria and dysentery, epidemic typhus among Korean coal miners and repatriates, and severe shortages of food, clothing, and housing, though per capita nutrition was targeted at 1,800 calories daily. For historians, this report is invaluable as a baseline inventory of Japan's devastated postwar welfare infrastructure, the early mechanics of SCAP indirect rule, the repatriation of roughly 150,000 Koreans, and emergency medical relief delivered to atomic bomb victims in Hiroshima.
